raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 'Lady-O' study (origin)
raw_evidence.content: This dataset was assembled by Jada Watson (a music industry researcher who runs SongData) and Jan Diehm of The Pudding for an article published May 2023 titled 'They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio: Examining Back-to-Back Plays by Gender, Race, and Sexual Orientation.' The team pulled 24-hour Mediabase logs from 29 large-market country radio stations, selecting 19 dates across 2022 — 12 month-end Fridays plus 7 dates that aligned with new releases by women artists, to give female songs the best possible chance of being heard. Each song was hand-coded by gender, race, and sexual orientation, then a script flagged every consecutive same-category pair — a back-to-back — for analysis. The whole point was to test whether country radio's long-rumored 'don't play two women in a row' rule was real, programmatic, and measurable.

raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the rule is named out loud (2015)
raw_evidence.content: In May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that programmers should not schedule two women back-to-back. His exact analogy: 'Trust me, I play great female records, and we've got some right now; they're just not the lettuce in our salad. The lettuce is Luke Bryan and Blake Shelton, Keith Urban and artists like that. The tomatoes of our salad are the females.' The remark — quickly nicknamed 'Tomato-gate' or 'SaladGate' — was the first time an unwritten programming rule passed around in country radio for decades was stated publicly and on the record. Martina McBride called it 'sexist and condescending'; Miranda Lambert called it 'bullshit' on Twitter; Jennifer Nettles, Reba McEntire, and Carrie Underwood all spoke out. The Pudding's 2022 dataset is the first attempt to actually measure whether the rule kept being followed in the eight years after Hill said it.

raw_evidence.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? At 17 of 29 stations, the answer was 'less often than chance' — meaning the observed pattern is not just under-representation, it is under-representation plus active separation. The men's number is the ceiling that lets us see how floor-low the women's number is.

raw_evidence.label: The headline asymmetry: 0.51% women b2b vs 65.01% men b2b
raw_evidence.content: Across the 182,848 plays in The Pudding's 29-station 2022 sample, songs by women appeared back-to-back 928 times — 0.51% of all plays. Songs by men appeared back-to-back 118,861 times — 65.01% of all plays. That is a 128-fold gap, even though men's airplay share (81.5%) is only about 8x women's airplay share (10.1%). The gap between the two ratios is the smoking gun: if back-to-backs scaled with airplay alone, the men:women b2b ratio would be roughly 64x, not 128x. Mixed-gender plays sit at 8.4% of plays and 0.47% as back-to-backs, behaving roughly like the women's number.
raw_evidence.code:
men = summary["onlyMenSongs_COUNT"].sum()
mixed = summary["onlyMixedGenderSongs_COUNT"].sum()
b2b_women = summary["b2bWomenSongs_COUNT"].sum()
b2b_men = summary["b2bMenSongs_COUNT"].sum()
b2b_mixed = summary["b2bMixedGenderSongs_COUNT"].sum()
print(f"Total plays across 29 stations (2022 sample): {total:,}")
print(f"Plays by women only:   {women:,} ({women/total*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Plays by men only:     {men:,} ({men/total*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Plays mixed-gender:    {mixed:,} ({mixed/total*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"Back-to-back women:    {b2b_women:,} ({b2b_women/total*100:.2f}% of all plays)")
print(f"Back-to-back men:      {b2b_men:,} ({b2b_men/total*100:.2f}% of all plays)")
print(f"Back-to-back mixed:    {b2b_mixed:,} ({b2b_mixed/total*100:.2f}% of all plays)")

# Ratios
print(f"\nMen's b2b rate is {b2b_men/b2b_women:.0f}x women's b2b rate")
print(f"Men's airplay share is {men/women:.1f}x women's airplay share")
# line ~30
raw_evidence.output:
Total plays across 29 stations (2022 sample): 182,848
Plays by women only:   18,412 (10.07%)
Plays by men only:     149,068 (81.53%)
Back-to-back women:    928 (0.51% of all plays)
Back-to-back men:      118,861 (65.01% of all plays)
Men's b2b rate is 128x women's b2b rate

raw_evidence.label: Hook — A song you cannot hear after another song
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: Numbers 0.51%, 65.01%, 128x, and 1,917x must appear exactly. The Hill quote should be verbatim. End the section on the WUBE 1,917x line — it is the punch.

raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the rule is named out loud (2015)
raw_evidence.content: In May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that programmers should not schedule two women back-to-back. His exact analogy: 'Trust me, I play great female records, and we've got some right now; they're just not the lettuce in our salad. The lettuce is Luke Bryan and Blake Shelton, Keith Urban and artists like that. The tomatoes of our salad are the females.' The remark — quickly nicknamed 'Tomato-gate' or 'SaladGate' — was the first time an unwritten programming rule passed around in country radio for decades was stated publicly and on the record. Martina McBride called it 'sexist and condescending'; Miranda Lambert called it 'bullshit' on Twitter; Jennifer Nettles, Reba McEntire, and Carrie Underwood all spoke out. The Pudding's 2022 dataset is the first attempt to actually measure whether the rule kept being followed in the eight years after Hill said it.

raw_evidence.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? At 17 of 29 stations, the answer was 'less often than chance' — meaning the observed pattern is not just under-representation, it is under-representation plus active separation. The men's number is the ceiling that lets us see how floor-low the women's number is.

raw_evidence.label: The headline asymmetry: 0.51% women b2b vs 65.01% men b2b

raw_evidence.label: The headline asymmetry: 0.51% women b2b vs 65.01% men b2b
raw_evidence.content: Across the 182,848 plays in The Pudding's 29-station 2022 sample, songs by women appeared back-to-back 928 times — 0.51% of all plays. raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the rule is named out loud (2015)
raw_evidence.content: In May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that programmers should not schedule two women back-to-back. His exact analogy: 'Trust me, I play great female records, and we've got some right now; they're just not the lettuce in our salad. The lettuce is Luke Bryan and Blake Shelton, Keith Urban and artists like that. The tomatoes of our salad are the females.' The remark — quickly nicknamed 'Tomato-gate' or 'SaladGate' — was the first time an unwritten programming rule passed around in country radio for decades was stated publicly and on the record. Martina McBride called it 'sexist and condescending'; Miranda Lambert called it 'bullshit' on Twitter; Jennifer Nettles, Reba McEntire, and Carrie Underwood all spoke out. The Pudding's 2022 dataset is the first attempt to actually measure whether the rule kept being followed in the eight years after Hill said it.

raw_evidence.label: The single worst station: Cincinnati's WUBE-FM, 2 b2bs in 6,221 plays
raw_evidence.content: WUBE-FM in Cincinnati (owner: Hubbard) is the format's outer floor. Across the 19 sampled days in 2022 the station played 6,221 songs, 648 of them by women (10.42% airplay share), and aired exactly two back-to-back women's pairs all year — 0.032%. The men's b2b rate at the same station was 61.61%. Put differently, this station produced one men's back-to-back roughly every 1.6 plays; one women's back-to-back roughly every 3,110 plays. The men's rate is 1,917 times the women's rate, the largest single-station ratio in the sample.

raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the rule is named out loud (2015)
raw_evidence.content: In May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that programmers should not schedule two women back-to-back. His exact analogy: 'Trust me, I play great female records, and we've got some right now; they're just not the lettuce in our salad. The lettuce is Luke Bryan and Blake Shelton, Keith Urban and artists like that. The tomatoes of our salad are the females.' The remark — quickly nicknamed 'Tomato-gate' or 'SaladGate' — was the first time an unwritten programming rule passed around in country radio for decades was stated publicly and on the record. Martina McBride called it 'sexist and condescending'; Miranda Lambert called it 'bullshit' on Twitter; Jennifer Nettles, Reba McEntire, and Carrie Underwood all spoke out. The Pudding's 2022 dataset is the first attempt to actually measure whether the rule kept being followed in the eight years after Hill said it.

raw_evidence.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? At 17 of 29 stations, the answer was 'less often than chance' — meaning the observed pattern is not just under-representation, it is under-representation plus active separation. The men's number is the ceiling that lets us see how floor-low the women's number is.

raw_evidence.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? raw_evidence.label: The 'flip the roles' counterfactual
raw_evidence.content: Watson and The Pudding ran a thought experiment as a sanity check: take each station's 24-hour log and swap every man's name with a woman's, holding everything else constant — the avoidance rule, the song-level slotting, the dayparting. The result is a hypothetical day where roughly 80% of slots are women. Even applying the same rule of 'don't play two women back-to-back' to that flipped log, women's back-to-backs would still appear at >25-30% of plays simply because there are not enough men to insert as separators. The actual observed women's back-to-back rate (~0.5%) is therefore impossible to produce without an active rule on top of the airplay-share imbalance. This is what 'systemic' means in the dataset: even after you account for the share, the gap is still bigger than chance.

raw_evidence.label: All 29 stations had observed b2b rates BELOW chance — and 18 below 0.001 chance
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding's permutation test took each station's 24-hour log, shuffled the order 1,000 times with no avoidance rule, and asked: how often does the simulated women's b2b rate fall as low as the observed rate? At 25 of 29 stations the observed value was below the 5th percentile of the simulated distribution (p < 0.05). At 20 stations p < 0.01. At 18 stations the p-value was zero — meaning the observed rate never occurred in 1,000 simulations of unrestricted programming. By the simpler back-of-envelope check (expected b2b under independence ≈ share²), all 29 stations come in below the chance baseline; the median observed/expected ratio is 0.51, and the worst-offending station's observed rate is 3% of the chance baseline. The pattern is not a side effect of women being rarer; it is an active separation rule on top of the rarity.

The result is a hypothetical day where roughly 80% of slots are women. Even applying the same rule of 'don't play two women back-to-back' to that flipped log, women's back-to-backs would still appear at >25-30% of plays simply because there are not enough men to insert as separators. The actual observed women's back-to-back rate (~0.5%) is therefore impossible to produce without an active rule on top of the airplay-share imbalance. This is what 'systemic' means in the dataset: even after you account for the share, the gap is still bigger than chance.

sources.title: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio (The Pudding)
facts: Reverse-roles simulation in the analysis directory of the dataset
Permutation tests at 1,000 iterations per station were used to measure deviation from chance

raw_evidence.label: All 29 stations had observed b2b rates BELOW chance — and 18 below 0.001 chance
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding's permutation test took each station's 24-hour log, shuffled the order 1,000 times with no avoidance rule, and asked: how often does the simulated women's b2b rate fall as low as the observed rate? At 25 of 29 stations the observed value was below the 5th percentile of the simulated distribution (p < 0.05). At 20 stations p < 0.01. At 18 stations the p-value was zero — meaning the observed rate never occurred in 1,000 simulations of unrestricted programming. By the simpler back-of-envelope check (expected b2b under independence ≈ share²), all 29 stations come in below the chance baseline; the median observed/expected ratio is 0.51, and the worst-offending station's observed rate is 3% of the chance baseline. The pattern is not a side effect of women being rarer; it is an active separation rule on top of the rarity.

print("=== ana_20 ===")

print()
print("p-value interpretation: probability that an unrestricted shuffle of the")
print("playlist produces a women's b2b rate as low as the observed value.")
print()
sig_05 = (pvals["pval_women"] < 0.05).sum()
sig_01 = (pvals["pval_women"] < 0.01).sum()
sig_001 = (pvals["pval_women"] < 0.001).sum()
zero_p = (pvals["pval_women"] == 0).sum()
print(f"Stations with p < 0.05  (observed rate is implausibly low under chance):  {sig_05} of {len(pvals)}")
print(f"Stations with p < 0.01:  {sig_01} of {len(pvals)}")
print(f"Stations with p < 0.001: {sig_001} of {len(pvals)}")
print(f"Stations with p = 0 (NEVER appeared in 1000 simulations of pure chance): {zero_p} of {len(pvals)}")
print()
print("Distribution of p-values:")
print(pvals["pval_women"].describe())

# --- ana_21: Per-station significance table ---
print("\n=== ana_21 ===")

print("\n=== ana_22 ===")
# Expected b2b rate under independence = (share)^2  approximately
expected = (summary["onlyWomenSongs_PERCENT"]/100) ** 2 * 100
observed = summary["b2bWomenSongs_PERCENT"]
ratio = observed / expected

station_compare["expected_b2b_pct_at_chance"] = expected.round(3)
station_compare["observed_b2b_pct"] = observed.round(3)

sentences.summary: det_08: Daypart trick: women on the graveyard shift. Source: Country Radio Plays Women Artists Back-to-Back Less Than 1% of Time (Billboard, May 2023) (https://www.billboard.com/pro/country-radio-plays-women-artists-back-to-back-1-p) Facts: 46.1% of women's back-to-back plays were in overnights (midnight-6 a.m.); 19% during evening hours (7 p.m.-midnight)

raw_evidence.label: Daypart trick: women on the graveyard shift
raw_evidence.content: When women are played, they are played when fewer people are listening. The Pudding piece reports that in 2022, 46.1% of women's back-to-back plays happened during overnights (midnight to 6 a.m.) and another 19% during evening hours (7 p.m. to midnight) — roughly 65% of women's back-to-backs concentrated in dayparts where listenership is at its weekly low. The morning drive (6-10 a.m. AMD) and afternoon drive (3-7 p.m. PMD), where ratings and ad revenue peak, are where men are stacked. This is the mechanism that makes the 11% airplay number even more punishing in practice: it is not 11% across the day, it is closer to 5% during the hours that count for ratings. Watson's broader work flags this as the practical translation of Hill's rule — women are not absent, they are quarantined.

raw_evidence.label: Race and queerness: a category of one
raw_evidence.content: Watson's coding tracks not just gender but race and sexual orientation. The race and orientation findings are the rawest in the dataset. In 2022, only 0.03% of plays on the 156 Mediabase-tracked stations went to Black or biracial women. LGBTQ+ artists collectively received 0.13% of airplay and the entire 2022 dataset contains a single back-to-back queer pair across 182,848 songs. The historical layer makes this concrete: Linda Martell remains the highest-charting Black woman in country history, with a 1969 chart entry that has never been surpassed; Crystal Shawanda was the last Indigenous woman to chart, in 2008; Mickey Guyton, the last Black woman to chart, did so in 2016. Asian women have never received country radio airplay; non-binary and trans artists are absent from the format entirely.

raw_evidence.label: Mickey Guyton's 'What Are You Gonna Tell Her' and 'Black Like Me'
raw_evidence.content: Mickey Guyton's 2020 song 'What Are You Gonna Tell Her' was performed at the Country Radio Seminar to a 2,400-strong audience of programmers and on-air talent — the people who decide who gets played. The song asks what a parent says to a Black girl when she discovers the country format will not give her the same chances it gives her white male peers. Variety called it country music's song of the year. Guyton's follow-up 'Black Like Me' became a Grammy nomination and a flagship example of country radio's race problem: the song was widely celebrated by critics, and barely played on country radio. Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio (The Pudding) (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: Women's back-to-backs are concentrated in 'gold' (older hits) and 'recurrent' tracks rather than 'current' songs; Top 3 current women artists make up 52.5% of all current women's airplay; top 3 men only 20.4%

raw_evidence.label: Glossary: gold, recurrent, current
raw_evidence.content: Country radio sorts every song into three programming buckets: 'current' (a recently released song actively being promoted), 'recurrent' (a song that just rotated off current and is still played for a few months), and 'gold' (an established hit, often years or decades old). These buckets matter because labels invest in promotion only when a song has a chance to chart — which means radio's behavior toward 'current' women's songs is the leading indicator of whether women still have a path. Watson's previous work, and the Pudding piece, both report that women's back-to-backs concentrate in 'gold' (older hits) rather than 'current' songs — meaning when a station does play two women in a row, it is usually a Reba McEntire/Faith Hill 'safe' pair, not two new artists in promotion. This is one reason the format keeps reproducing itself: new women never get the spin density needed to become the next safe gold pair five years from now.

raw_evidence.label: The bottleneck: 3 women hold 52.2% of all current-women's airplay
raw_evidence.content: In 2022's 'current' rotation — songs labels are actively promoting to chart — there are 35 unique women artists and 158 unique men artists across all 29 stations. The top three women (Gabby Barrett, Kelsea Ballerini, Lainey Wilson) collected 1,697 of the 3,254 women's current plays — 52.2%. The top three men (Jelly Roll, Jimmie Allen, Zac Brown Band) collected 2,158 of 10,617 men's current plays — 20.3%. Among women in the current rotation, just three artists do two-thirds of the work that 35 artists are nominally on the bench for. This is the bottleneck The Pudding describes: three women's careers stand in for the entire format's progress narrative.

# --- ana_16: Top current women — concentration in three artists ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
women = raw[raw["gender"]=="women"]
current_women = women[women["grc"]=="C"]
total_current_women = len(current_women)
women_artist_counts = current_women.groupby("artist").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
top10_w = women_artist_counts.head(10)
top3_w = women_artist_counts.head(3)
print(f"Total current-bucket women plays in 2022 sample: {total_current_women}")
print(f"Unique women artists in current rotation: {women_artist_counts.shape[0]}")
print(f"\nTop 10 current women artists:")
for artist, count in top10_w.items():
    print(f"  {artist:30s} {count:>4}  ({count/total_current_women*100:5.1f}%)")
print(f"\nTop 3 current women artists account for {top3_w.sum()} / {total_current_women} = {top3_w.sum()/total_current_women*100:.1f}% of current women's plays")
# line ~25

# --- ana_17: Top current men — much flatter distribution ---
print("\n=== ana_17 ===")
men = raw[raw["gender"]=="men"]
current_men = men[men["grc"]=="C"]
total_current_men = len(current_men)
men_artist_counts = current_men.groupby("artist").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
top10_m = men_artist_counts.head(10)
top3_m = men_artist_counts.head(3)
print(f"Total current-bucket men plays: {total_current_men}")
print(f"Unique men artists in current rotation: {men_artist_counts.shape[0]}")
print(f"\nTop 10 current men artists:")
for artist, count in top10_m.items():
    print(f"  {artist:30s} {count:>4}  ({count/total_current_men*100:5.1f}%)")
print(f"\nTop 3 current men artists account for {top3_m.sum()} / {total_current_men} = {top3_m.sum()/total_current_men*100:.1f}% of current men's plays")
print(f"\nConcentration ratio: women's top-3 dominance is {top3_w.sum()/total_current_women / (top3_m.sum()/total_current_men):.2f}x men's")

sentences.summary: det_07: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark. Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio (The Pudding) (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: Men's back-to-back rate is roughly 60-65% across stations; 1,000-iteration permutation test on each station's 24-hour log

raw_evidence.label: Reverse roles: men's back-to-back rate as a benchmark
raw_evidence.content: The Pudding piece reports that across the 29-station sample, songs by men were played back-to-back roughly 60-65% of the time. That is not a coincidence — it is the mathematical expectation of a format where ~80% of plays are by men. If a station played randomly with no avoidance, women's back-to-back rate would float around 1-2% (the square of women's airplay share). The Pudding's permutation test shuffled each station's 24-hour log 1,000 times, with no avoidance rule applied, and asked: how often do you see a women's back-to-back rate as low as the observed one? At 17 of 29 stations, the answer was 'less often than chance' — meaning the observed pattern is not just under-representation, it is under-representation plus active separation. The men's number is the ceiling that lets us see how floor-low the women's number is.

raw_evidence.label: Why women's airplay matters: the career-stack consequence
raw_evidence.content: Country radio is not just one input among many — it is the gate that controls almost everything else. Airplay drives chart position; chart position drives label promotion budgets; promotion drives festival bookings, award eligibility (the CMAs, ACMs and Grammy country categories all weigh radio activity), and tour revenue. When women receive only 11% of airplay, every downstream system inherits that floor: smaller advances, fewer single releases, fewer label signings, fewer slots at the Opry and at country festivals. Brandi Carlile, in a widely cited interview tied to the Pudding piece, framed the stakes as generational: 'What does that say to a 10-year-old girl about life?' The point of measuring back-to-back rates is not curiosity — it is showing that the upstream constraint is still active.

raw_evidence.label: The historical baseline: women's share of country radio over 50 years
raw_evidence.content: Women's share of country radio is not at a normal-low; it is at a historical low. Watson's earlier SongData research, the 2019 'Gender Representation on Country Format Radio' report, traced women on the Billboard Country Airplay chart from 1969 to 2019 and found peaks of 33.1% in 1999 and a steady decline to 11.4% in 2015 — the year of Hill's 'tomato' quote. By 2022 it averaged roughly 15% but back-to-back women plays specifically remained around 0.5%. This long sweep matters because it shows the back-to-back rule is not the whole story: the share started shrinking before 2015 and continued shrinking after. Tomato-gate is a symptom, not the cause.

raw_evidence.label: Why women's airplay matters: the career-stack consequence
raw_evidence.content: Country radio is not just one input among many — it is the gate that controls almost everything else. Airplay drives chart position; chart position drives label promotion budgets; promotion drives festival bookings, award eligibility (the CMAs, ACMs and Grammy country categories all weigh radio activity), and tour revenue. When women receive only 11% of airplay, every downstream system inherits that floor: smaller advances, fewer single releases, fewer label signings, fewer slots at the Opry and at country festivals. Brandi Carlile, in a widely cited interview tied to the Pudding piece, framed the stakes as generational: 'What does that say to a 10-year-old girl about life?' The point of measuring back-to-back rates is not curiosity — it is showing that the upstream constraint is still active.

raw_evidence.label: The historical baseline: women's share of country radio over 50 years
raw_evidence.content: Women's share of country radio is not at a normal-low; it is at a historical low. Watson's earlier SongData research, the 2019 'Gender Representation on Country Format Radio' report, traced women on the Billboard Country Airplay chart from 1969 to 2019 and found peaks of 33.1% in 1999 and a steady decline to 11.4% in 2015 — the year of Hill's 'tomato' quote. By 2022 it averaged roughly 15% but back-to-back women plays specifically remained around 0.5%. This long sweep matters because it shows the back-to-back rule is not the whole story: the share started shrinking before 2015 and continued shrinking after. Tomato-gate is a symptom, not the cause.

raw_evidence.label: The bottleneck: 3 women hold 52.2% of all current-women's airplay
raw_evidence.content: In 2022's 'current' rotation — songs labels are actively promoting to chart — there are 35 unique women artists and 158 unique men artists across all 29 stations. The top three women (Gabby Barrett, Kelsea Ballerini, Lainey Wilson) collected 1,697 of the 3,254 women's current plays — 52.2%. The top three men (Jelly Roll, Jimmie Allen, Zac Brown Band) collected 2,158 of 10,617 men's current plays — 20.3%. Among women in the current rotation, just three artists do two-thirds of the work that 35 artists are nominally on the bench for. This is the bottleneck The Pudding describes: three women's careers stand in for the entire format's progress narrative.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_16: Top current women — concentration in three artists ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
women = raw[raw["gender"]=="women"]
current_women = women[women["grc"]=="C"]
total_current_women = len(current_women)
women_artist_counts = current_women.groupby("artist").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
top10_w = women_artist_counts.head(10)
top3_w = women_artist_counts.head(3)
print(f"Total current-bucket women plays in 2022 sample: {total_current_women}")
print(f"Unique women artists in current rotation: {women_artist_counts.shape[0]}")
print(f"\nTop 10 current women artists:")
for artist, count in top10_w.items():
    print(f"  {artist:30s} {count:>4}  ({count/total_current_women*100:5.1f}%)")
print(f"\nTop 3 current women artists account for {top3_w.sum()} / {total_current_women} = {top3_w.sum()/total_current_women*100:.1f}% of current women's plays")
# line ~25

# --- ana_17: Top current men — much flatter distribution ---
print("\n=== ana_17 ===")
men = raw[raw["gender"]=="men"]
current_men = men[men["grc"]=="C"]
total_current_men = len(current_men)
men_artist_counts = current_men.groupby("artist").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
top10_m = men_artist_counts.head(10)
top3_m = men_artist_counts.head(3)
print(f"Total current-bucket men plays: {total_current_men}")
print(f"Unique men artists in current rotation: {men_artist_counts.shape[0]}")
print(f"\nTop 10 current men artists:")
for artist, count in top10_m.items():
    print(f"  {artist:30s} {count:>4}  ({count/total_current_men*100:5.1f}%)")
print(f"\nTop 3 current men artists account for {top3_m.sum()} / {total_current_men} = {top3_m.sum()/total_current_men*100:.1f}% of current men's plays")
print(f"\nConcentration ratio: women's top-3 dominance is {top3_w.sum()/total_current_women / (top3_m.sum()/total_current_men):.2f}x men's")

# --- ana_18: All POC women in the 2022 dataset ---
print("\n=== ana_18 ===")
